procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Allahabad High Court (S. D. Singh J) dated April 16, 1968, which quashed the proceedings in the court of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Brij Mohan Chandra applied to the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad under s. 561A, Cr. P.C. for quashing the proceedings in the court of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate. The High Court quashed the proceedings, holding that the levy was outside the Act and s. 164 of the Act could not bar the High Court's jurisdiction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Municipal Board appealed the High Court's decision to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision that the levy was ultra vires the taxing power of the Board.

issue.issue_text: Whether toll-tax on laden motor vehicles levied under s. 128 (1)(vii) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916 on their entry within the limits of a Municipality can be realised from the passengers carried by them.

facts: The Municipal Board of Nainital levied a toll-tax on laden motor vehicles entering its limits, as authorized by s. 128 (1)(vii) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916.
The municipality attempted to collect this toll-tax from the passengers travelling within these vehicles.
The appellants argued that the tax could be collected from passengers because of their 'nexus' with the entry of the vehicle.
law: Section 128(1)(vii) of the Act authorizes a toll on 'vehicles and other conveyances... entering the municipality.'
The Rules made under the Act for the collection of tolls state that the toll on a laden motor vehicle is to be paid by the 'person-in-charge of the vehicle.'
A separate provision in the Rules states that a 'toll on a passenger is to be paid by the passenger.'
application: The Court first determined that the authorizing law, s. 128(1)(vii), is 'clear and unambiguous' in that it allows a tax on vehicles, but does not authorize a tax on passengers. The appellants conceded this point.
The Court then examined the collection rules. It found that the rules explicitly state that the toll imposed on a laden vehicle is 'expressly made payable by the person-in-charge of such vehicles.'

The Court reasoned that the rule allowing collection of a 'toll on a passenger' from the passenger was irrelevant, because it only applies if a toll has been legally imposed on passengers in the first place, which was not the case here.
The Court found no legal basis, precedent, or principle to support the argument that a tax imposed on a vehicle could be demanded from its passengers simply because they were being carried by it.
Since the law imposed the tax on the vehicle and the rules fixed the liability for payment on the person-in-charge, the Court found no legal ground to demand payment from the passengers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the toll-tax levied on the vehicles could not be legally realised from the passengers carried by them, as the liability for the tax was explicitly placed on the person-in-charge of the vehicle, not the passengers.

issue.issue_text: Whether section 164 of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916 could operate to bar the jurisdiction of the High Court to quash a levy which is ultra vires the taxing power of the Board under the Act.

facts: The appellant (the Municipal Board) made a final argument that section 164 of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, barred the High Court's jurisdiction to hear the case and quash the proceedings related to the toll-tax levy.
law: A provision within a statute that bars a court's jurisdiction, such as section 164, does not apply if the action being challenged (in this case, a tax levy) is itself outside the legal authority granted by that statute (i.e., it is 'ultra vires').
application: The court found that the argument made by the appellant ignored the "vital point" that the tax levy on passengers was 'ultra vires' the taxing power of the Board and therefore outside the Act itself.
Because the levy was outside the Act, the provisions of the Act, including the jurisdictional bar in section 164, could not be used to protect that illegal levy.
The court reasoned that the High Court's power to quash proceedings for a levy that is ultra vires cannot be taken away by a section of the very Act that the levy violates.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that because the tax levy on passengers was ultra vires the Board's power, section 164 of the Act could not operate to bar the High Court's jurisdiction to quash the illegal proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether toll-tax on laden motor vehicles levied under s. 128 (1)(vii) of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916 on their entry within the limits of a Municipality can be realised from the passengers carried by them.
appellant_arguments: The toll imposed on a vehicle entering the municipality could legally be realised from the passengers it carried because of the passengers' nexus with the entry of the vehicle.
An initial, but later abandoned, argument was that the levy on passengers was valid under clause (xiv) of s. 128(1).
respondent_arguments: The Act (s. 128(1)) and the relevant notification only authorized a toll-tax on vehicles, not on passengers. Therefore, any rule imposing an obligation on passengers to pay the toll is ultra vires (beyond the legal power) of the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether section 164 of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916 could operate to bar the jurisdiction of the High Court to quash a levy which is ultra vires the taxing power of the Board under the Act.
appellant_arguments: Section 164 of the Act bars the jurisdiction of the High Court from entertaining the petition and holding the assessment to be illegal.
respondent_arguments: The bar on jurisdiction under Section 164 does not apply if the levy is ultra vires (outside the power of) the Act. The court's power to quash a levy that is fundamentally illegal and not authorized by the Act cannot be taken away.

statutes.act_name: Rules for the assessment and collection of tolls in the Nainital Municipality (made under s. 153(a) and s. 296 of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A tax imposed on passengers is legally incompetent and ultra vires if the enabling statute only authorizes the levy of a toll on vehicles. Liability for a toll tax imposed on a vehicle cannot be demanded from its passengers in the absence of a specific statutory provision creating such liability.
obiter: A statutory provision barring a court's jurisdiction to challenge a tax levy cannot operate when the impugned levy is outside the scope of the authorizing statute itself.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916, specifically s. 128(1)(vii), authorizes a toll-tax on vehicles entering a municipality, not on the passengers they carry. Any rule or action by the Municipal Board to realize this vehicle-specific tax from passengers is therefore ultra vires (beyond its legal power) and incompetent. Consequently, a statutory provision like s. 164, which bars challenges to assessments, cannot operate to prevent a High Court from exercising its jurisdiction to quash a levy that is fundamentally illegal and outside the authority granted by the Act itself.
legal_tests_applied: Ultra Vires Doctrine: The court assessed whether the Municipal Board's action of levying a toll on passengers exceeded the express taxing powers granted to it by the enabling statute, the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1916.

Statutory Interpretation: The court conducted a plain reading of s. 128(1)(vii) of the Act to determine the scope of the authorized tax, concluding it was limited to vehicles and did not extend to passengers.

Jurisdictional Bar Exception: The court applied the principle that a statutory bar to judicial review does not apply when the administrative body's action is wholly without jurisdiction or ultra vires the statute from which it purports to derive its power.
why_appellant_lost: The court found that s. 128(1)(vii) of the Act, in 'clear and unambiguous terms speaks of a toll on· vehicles' and 'does not take within its fold the passengers carried by vehicles to be taxed'.

The appellant's argument of a 'nexus' between the passengers and the vehicle's entry was rejected as the court was not invited to 'any provision of Jaw under which the passengers can be held liable to pay the toll-tax imposed on the vehicles.'
The appellant failed to cite any precedent or legal principle to support the submission that a tax on a vehicle could be demanded from its passengers.
The argument that s. 164 of the Act barred the High Court's jurisdiction was dismissed because it 'ignores the vital point that if the impugned levv is outside the Act' then the bar cannot apply.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed with the respondent's core contention that the levy of toll-tax on passengers was 'ultra vires the taxing power of the Board' under the Act.

The court affirmed the High Court's finding that the relevant notification levied tax only on vehicles and not on passengers, and therefore any rule imposing an obligation on passengers to pay was invalid.

The respondent's argument that the jurisdictional bar in s. 164 does not apply to an ultra vires levy was accepted, with the court stating that the power 'to quash the proceedings relating to the levy which is ultra vir~s the taxing power of the Board UI1der the Act cannot be taken away'.
policy_considerations: The court implicitly endorsed the policy of protecting citizens from illegal taxation by affirming that the High Court's power to quash an ultra vires levy 'cannot be taken away to the prejudice of the aggrieved citizen.'
